questions.question: Let \(h(t)\) denote the impulse response of a causal system with transfer function \(\frac{1}{s+1}\). Consider the following three statements. S1 : The system is stable S2: \(\frac{h(t+1)}{h(t)}\) is independent of \(t > 0\) S3 : A non-causal system with the same transfer function is stable For the above system
options: only S1 and S2 are true
only S2 and S3 are true
only S1 and S3 are true
questions.explanation:
Given \(H(s) = \frac{1}{(s + 1)}\) \[h(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\] at \(t = \infty, h(t) = 0\) i.e. the system is stable as it converges to zero as \(t \to \infty\). The system is causal as it can be seen from the graph that \(h(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\). \[\frac{h(t+1)}{h(t)} = \frac{e^{-(t+1)}}{e^{-t}} = \frac{e^{-t} \cdot e^{-1}}{e^{-t}}\] \[= e^{-1} \text{ i.e. independent of t}\] So, statements \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are true. \[\boxed{\text{A) only S1 and S2 are true }}\]
Key points
  • Stability: A causal LTI system is bounded-input bounded-output (BIBO) stable if its impulse response is absolutely integrable (\(\int_0^\infty |h(t)| dt < \infty\)). For \(h(t) = e^{-t}u(t)\), the integral evaluates to \(1\), hence it is stable.
  • Causality: A continuous-time LTI system is causal if and only if its impulse response \(h(t) = 0\) for \(t < 0\). The presence of the unit step function \(u(t)\) guarantees this condition.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A system is described by the following differential equation, where \(u(t)\) is the input to the system and \(y(t)\) is the output of the system. \[\dot{y}(t) + 5y(t) = u(t)\] When \(y(0) = 1\) and \(u(t)\) is a unit step function, \(y(t)\) is
questions.explanation:
Given \(\dot{y}(t) + 5y(t) = u(t)\) and \(y(0)=1\); \(u(t)\) is a unit step function. Apply Laplace transform to the given differential equation. \[s y(s) - y(0) + 5y(s) = \frac{1}{s}\] \[y(s)[s + 5] = \frac{1}{s} + y(0) \quad \left[ \mathcal{L}\left[\frac{dy}{dt}\right] = s y(s) - y(0) \right] \left[ \mathcal{L}\left[u(t)\right] = \frac{1}{s} \right]\] \[y(s) = \frac{\frac{1}{s} + 1}{(s + 5)}\] \[y(s) = \frac{(s + 1)}{s(s + 5)} \Rightarrow \frac{A}{s} + \frac{B}{s + 5}\] \(A = 1/5\); \(B = 4/5\) \[y(s) = \frac{1}{5s} + \frac{4}{5(s + 5)}\] Apply inverse Laplace transform, \[y(t) = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{4}{5}e^{-5t}\] \[y(t) = 0.2 + 0.8e^{-5t}\] \[\boxed{\text{A) $0.2 + 0.8e^{-5t}$ }}\]
Key points
  • Laplace Transform of a Derivative: \(\mathcal{L}\{\dot{y}(t)\} = sY(s) - y(0)\).
  • Laplace Transform of Unit Step: \(\mathcal{L}\{u(t)\} = \frac{1}{s}\).
  • Partial Fraction Expansion: Used to split complex rational fractions into simpler terms for straightforward inverse Laplace transformation.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The input \(-3e^{2t}u(t)\), where \(u(t)\) is the unit step function, is applied to a system with transfer function \(\frac{s-2}{s+3}\). If the initial value of the output is \(-2\), then the value of the output at steady state is _____.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A continuous, linear time-invariant filter has an impulse response \(h(t)\) described by \[h(t) = \begin{cases} 3 & \text{for } 0 \le t \le 3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\] When a constant input of value \(5\) is applied to this filter, the steady state output is _______.
questions.explanation:
If the input is \(ke^{st}\) then the output is \(ke^{st} H(s)\). \[h(t) = 3 [u(t) - u(t - 3)]\] By applying Laplace Transform, \[H(s) = 3 \left[ \frac{1 - e^{-3s}}{s} \right]\] We can take the input as \(5e^{0\cdot t}\) which means \(s = 0\). Then the output is \[y(t) = 5 \lim_{s \to 0} H(s) = \left. 5(3)(3)e^{-3s} \right|_{s=0} = 45\] \[\boxed{45}\]
Key points
  • Eigenfunction Property: For an LTI system, complex exponentials are eigenfunctions. An input \(x(t) = e^{st}\) produces a steady-state output \(y(t) = H(s)e^{st}\). A constant DC input is a special case where \(s=0\).
  • DC Gain: The steady-state response to a constant input \(A\) is \(A \cdot H(0)\). The DC gain \(H(0)\) can be evaluated using L'Hôpital's rule on the transfer function, or alternatively, by finding the total area under the impulse response curve directly (\(3 \times 3 = 9\)).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The z-transform of the sequence \(x[n]\) is given by \(X(z) = \frac{1}{(1-2z^{-1})^2}\), with the region of convergence \(|z| > 2\). Then, \(x[2]\) is _____.
questions.explanation:
Given, \[X(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - 2z^{-1})^2}, \quad |Z| > 2\] \[X(z) = (1 - 2z^{-1})^{-2}\] \[X(z) = 1 + 4z^{-1} + 12z^{-2} + \dots\] (using binomial expansion) Taking inverse z-transform, we get \[\therefore \quad x[n] = \{ 1, \ 4, \ 12, \ \dots \}\] \[x[2] = \boxed{12}\]
Key points
  • The region of convergence \(|Z| > 2\) indicates a right-sided (causal) sequence, meaning the Z-transform can be expanded as a power series in negative powers of \(z\).
  • The binomial expansion formula \((1 - x)^{-2} = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3 + \dots\) is applied to expand the rational function.
  • By definition, \(X(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x[n]z^{-n}\). Matching the coefficients from the series expansion directly provides the sequence values, where the coefficient of \(z^{-2}\) is \(x[2]\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Let \(H_1(z) = (1 - pz^{-1})^{-1}\), \(H_2(z) = (1 - qz^{-1})^{-1}\), \(H(z) = H_1(z) + rH_2(z)\). The quantities \(p\), \(q\), \(r\) are real numbers. Consider \(p = \frac{1}{2}\), \(q = -\frac{1}{4}\), \(|r| < 1\). If the zero of \(H(z)\) lies on the unit circle, then \(r =\) _______.
questions.explanation:
Here \(H_1(z) = \frac{1}{1 - pz^{-1}}\) \[H_2(z) = \frac{1}{1 - qz^{-1}}\] also \(p = \frac{1}{2}, \ q = -\frac{1}{4}\) \[\therefore \quad H(z) = H_1(z) + rH_2(z)\] \[= \frac{1}{1 - pz^{-1}} + \frac{r}{1 - qz^{-1}}\] \[= \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}z^{-1}} + \frac{r}{1 + \frac{1}{4}z^{-1}}\] \[H(z) = \frac{(1 + \frac{1}{4}z^{-1}) + r(1 - \frac{1}{2}z^{-1})}{(1 - \frac{1}{2}z^{-1})(1 + \frac{1}{4}z^{-1})} \dots(i)\] zero of \(H(z) \Rightarrow\) \[(1 + r) - (q + pr)z^{-1} = 0 \dots(ii)\] or \(\quad z = \frac{q + pr}{1 + r}\) Since, the zero of \(H(z)\) lies on the unit circle therefore \(|z| = 1\) or \(z = \pm 1\) Taking \(z=1\), we get \[z = \frac{q + pr}{1 + r} = 1 \dots(iii)\] By solving above expression with \(p = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(q = -\frac{1}{4}\), we get \[r = -2.5\] But \(|r| < 1 \quad \text{or} \quad -1 < r < 1\) Taking \(z=-1\) in equation (iii), we get \[\boxed{r = -0.5}\]
Key points
  • The zeros of a rational transfer function \(H(z)\) are the roots of its numerator polynomial.
  • For a zero to lie on the unit circle, its magnitude must be \(1\) (i.e., \(|z| = 1\), which implies \(z = 1\) or \(z = -1\) for strictly real coefficients).
  • Applying the given condition \(|r| < 1\) acts as a mathematical constraint to filter out invalid roots, ensuring the correct parameter value is selected.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The input-output relationship of a causal stable LTI system is given as \(y[n] = \alpha y[n - 1]+ \beta x[n]\) If the impulse response \(h[n]\) of this system satisfies the con dition \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h[n] = 2\), the relationship between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is
questions.explanation:
Input-output relation is given as \[y[n] = \alpha y(n - 1) + \beta x[n]\] Taking Z-transform, \[Y(z) = \alpha z^{-1} Y(z) + \beta X(z)\] \[Y(z) [1 - \alpha z^{-1}] = \beta X(z)\] \[\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)} = H(z) = \frac{\beta}{1 - \alpha z^{-1}}\] \[h[n] = \beta \cdot \alpha^n u[n]\] Also \[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h[n] = 2 \Rightarrow \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \beta \cdot \alpha^n u[n] = 2\] \[\frac{\beta}{1 - \alpha} = 2 \Rightarrow \beta = 2 - 2\alpha\] \[\Rightarrow 2\alpha = 2 - \beta\] \[\boxed{\text{A) }\alpha = 1 - \frac{\beta}{2}}\]
Key points
  • The Z-transform converts a time-domain difference equation into an algebraic equation, using the time-shifting property where a delay of 1 sample (\(y[n-1]\)) corresponds to multiplication by \(z^{-1}\).
  • The transfer function \(H(z)\) of the LTI system is defined as the ratio \(\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}\).
  • The infinite sum of the impulse response sequence \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} h[n]\) is mathematically equivalent to evaluating the transfer function at \(z = 1\) (the DC gain of the system). Setting \(H(1) = 2\) directly yields the relation between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Let \(x[n] = \left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)^n u(n) - \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^n u(-n - 1)\). The Region of Convergence (ROC) of the z -transform of x[n].
questions.explanation:
\[x(n) = \underbrace{\left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)^n u(n)}_{x_1(n)} - \underbrace{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^n u(-n - 1)}_{x_2(n)}\] \[x_1(n) = \left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)^n u(n) \rightarrow \text{Right sided signal}\] \[x_1(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)z^{-1}}\] \[\text{ROC } |z| \geq \left|\frac{1}{9}\right| \text{ or } |z| > \frac{1}{9}\] \[x_2(n) = \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^n u(-n - 1) \rightarrow \text{Left sided signal}\] \[x_2(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)z^{-1}}; \quad |z| < \frac{1}{3}\] Now, when both the transforms are added using linearity property. ROC must be between \[\boxed{\text{C) }\frac{1}{3} > |z| > \frac{1}{9}}\]
Key points
  • The Z-transform of a right-sided sequence \(a^n u(n)\) is \(\frac{1}{1-az^{-1}}\) with ROC \(|z| > |a|\).
  • The Z-transform of a left-sided sequence \(-b^n u(-n-1)\) is \(\frac{1}{1-bz^{-1}}\) with ROC \(|z| < |b|\).
  • By the linearity property, the ROC of the sum of two signals is the intersection of their individual ROCs.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Let \(x[n] = x[-n]\). Let \(X(z)\) be the z -transform of \(x[n]\). If \(0.5+j0.25\) is a zero of \(X(z)\), which one of the following must also be a zero of \(X(z)\).
questions.explanation:
Given \(x[n] = x[-n]\) As we know that, \[x[n] \stackrel{Z}{\longleftrightarrow} X[z]\] \[x[-n] \stackrel{Z}{\longleftrightarrow} X[z^{-1}]\] So, when \((0.5 + j0.25)\) is a zero of \(X(z)\). Now \(x[-n] \longleftrightarrow X(z^{-1})\) \[\text{Zero of } X(z) = \frac{1}{(0.5+j0.25)}\] \[\boxed{\text{B) }\frac{1}{0.5+j0.25}}\]
Key points
  • The time-reversal property of the Z-transform states that if a sequence is time-reversed (\(x[-n]\)), its Z-transform domain variable is inverted (\(z^{-1}\)).
  • For an even symmetric signal where \(x[n] = x[-n]\), its Z-transform must satisfy \(X(z) = X(z^{-1})\).
  • Consequently, if a system possesses a zero at a complex location \(z_0\), it must inherently have a corresponding zero at the reciprocal location \(1/z_0\) to preserve this symmetry.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: For an all-pass system \(H(z) = \frac{(z^{-1}-b)}{(1-az^{-1})}\), where \(|H(e^{-j\omega})| = 1\), for all \(\omega\). If \(\text{Re}(a) \neq 0\), \(\text{Im}(a) \neq 0\), then b equals
questions.explanation:
For the given system \[H(z) = \frac{(z^{-1}-b)}{(1-az^{-1})}\] The pole lie at \(z=a\) and the zero lie at \(z = \frac{1}{b}\) also 'a' is complex in nature. Thus, \(a = |a|e^{j\angle a}\) For an all pass system where \(|H(e^{-j\omega})| = 1\), for all \(\omega\), if the pole lies at 'a' then the zero must be present at \(\frac{1}{a^*}\) \[\therefore \quad \left(\frac{1}{b}\right) = \frac{1}{|a|e^{-j\angle a}} = \frac{1}{a^*}\] \[\text{or} \quad \boxed{B) b = a^*}\]
Key points
  • A discrete-time all-pass system is characterized by a constant magnitude response across all frequencies, i.e., \(|H(e^{j\omega})| = 1\).
  • To satisfy this condition, the poles and zeros of the transfer function \(H(z)\) must exist in conjugate reciprocal pairs. Specifically, a pole at \(z = p\) necessitates a zero at \(z = 1/p^*\).
  • By matching the given transfer function's zero location (\(1/b\)) to the theoretically required zero location (\(1/a^*\)), the relationship between the parameters is established.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: An FIR system is described by the system function \[H(z) = 1 + \frac{7}{2}z^{-1} + \frac{3}{2}z^{-2}\]
questions.explanation:
Given system function: \[H(z) = 1 + \frac{7}{2}z^{-1} + \frac{3}{2}z^{-2}\] To find the zeros of the system, equate \(H(z)\) to \(0\): \[1 + \frac{7}{2}z^{-1} + \frac{3}{2}z^{-2} = 0\] Multiplying by \(2z^2\), we get the characteristic equation: \[2z^2 + 7z + 3 = 0\] \[2z^2 + 6z + z + 3 = 0\] \[2z(z + 3) + 1(z + 3) = 0\] \[(2z + 1)(z + 3) = 0\] The zeros are located at \(z = -1/2\) and \(z = -3\). Since one zero (\(z = -1/2\)) lies inside the unit circle (\(|z| < 1\)) and the other zero (\(z = -3\)) lies outside the unit circle (\(|z| > 1\)), the system is a mixed phase system. \[\boxed{\text{C) mixed phase }}\]
Key points
  • Minimum Phase System: All zeros of the transfer function lie strictly inside the unit circle.
  • Maximum Phase System: All zeros of the transfer function lie strictly outside the unit circle.
  • Mixed Phase System: The zeros are distributed both inside and outside the unit circle.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The sequence \(x[n] = 0.5^n u[n]\), where \(u[n]\) is the unit step sequence, is convolved with itself to obtain \(y[n]\). Then \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} y[n]\) is _________.
questions.explanation:
Given sequence, \[x[n] = 0.5^n u[n]\] The sequence \(y[n]\) is obtained by convolving \(x[n]\) with itself: \[y[n] = x[n] * x[n]\] Taking the Z-transform on both sides, we get: \[Y(z) = X(z) \cdot X(z) = [X(z)]^2\] The Z-transform of the standard sequence \(a^n u[n]\) is \(\frac{1}{1 - az^{-1}}\). Thus, for \(x[n]\): \[X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - 0.5z^{-1}}\] We know that the sum of all samples of a sequence from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\) is equal to its Z-transform evaluated at \(z = 1\): \[\sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} y[n] = Y(z)\Big|_{z=1} = Y(1)\] First, evaluate \(X(z)\) at \(z = 1\): \[X(1) = \frac{1}{1 - 0.5(1)^{-1}} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.5} = \frac{1}{0.5} = 2\] Now, calculate \(Y(1)\): \[Y(1) = [X(1)]^2 = (2)^2 = 4\] \[\boxed{4}\]
Key points
  • Convolution in the time domain corresponds to multiplication in the Z-domain: \(y[n] = x_1[n] * x_2[n] \leftrightarrow Y(z) = X_1(z)X_2(z)\).
  • The sum of the samples of a discrete-time signal is equivalent to its Z-transform evaluated at \(z=1\), given by the property: \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n] = X(e^{j0}) = X(1)\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Consider a discrete time periodic signal \(x[n] = \sin \left( \frac{\pi n}{5} \right)\). Let \(a_k\) be the complex Fourier serier coefficients of \(x[n]\). The coefficients \(\{a_k\}\) are non- zero when \(k = Bm \pm 1\), where \(m\) is any integer. The value of B is .
questions.explanation:
Given the discrete-time periodic signal: \[x[n] = \sin\left(\frac{\pi n}{5}\right)\] First, determine the fundamental period (\(N\)) of the signal. The fundamental angular frequency is \(\Omega_0 = \frac{\pi}{5}\). For a discrete-time signal to be periodic, the ratio \(\frac{2\pi}{\Omega_0}\) must be a rational number of the form \(\frac{N}{m}\), where \(N\) and \(m\) are integers. \[\frac{N}{m} = \frac{2\pi}{\pi/5} = 10\] To find the fundamental period, we choose the smallest integer \(m\) that makes \(N\) an integer. Setting \(m = 1\), we get the fundamental period \(N = 10\). Using Euler's identity, we can expand the signal into its complex exponential form: \[x[n] = \frac{1}{2j}\exp\left(j\frac{\pi}{5}n\right) - \frac{1}{2j}\exp\left(-j\frac{\pi}{5}n\right)\] The standard Discrete Fourier Series (DFS) synthesis equation for a signal with period \(N=10\) is: \[x[n] = \sum_{k=\langle 10 \rangle} a_k \exp\left(j k \Omega_0 n\right) = \sum_{k=\langle 10 \rangle} a_k \exp\left(j k \frac{\pi}{5} n\right)\] By comparing the terms of our expanded signal with the standard DFS equation, we can identify the non-zero coefficients within the principal period (where \(k = 1\) and \(k = -1\)): \[a_1 = \frac{1}{2j}\] \[a_{-1} = -\frac{1}{2j}\] A fundamental property of DFS coefficients is that they are periodic with the same period \(N\) as the time-domain signal. Therefore: \[a_k = a_{k \pm mN}\] where \(m\) is any integer. Since the non-zero coefficients occur at \(k = 1\) and \(k = -1\), and the period is \(N = 10\), the complete set of non-zero coefficients \(\{a_k\}\) will occur at: \[k = 10m + 1\] \[k = 10m - 1\] Combining these, the non-zero coefficients exist when \(k = 10m \pm 1\). Comparing this result with the given generalized condition \(k = Bm \pm 1\), we find: \[B = 10\] \[\boxed{10}\]
Key points
  • Euler's identity for sine: \(\sin(\theta) = \frac{e^{j\theta} - e^{-j\theta}}{2j}\)
  • Periodicity of discrete signals: A discrete sinusoid \(\sin(\Omega_0 n)\) is periodic if \(\frac{2\pi}{\Omega_0} = \frac{N}{m}\). The fundamental period \(N\) is the smallest integer satisfying this relation.
  • Periodicity of DFS coefficients: The DFS coefficients \(a_k\) of a periodic sequence with period \(N\) form a periodic sequence with the same period \(N\), such that \(a_k = a_{k+mN}\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The N-point DFT \(X\) of a sequence \(x[n]\) \(0 \le n \le N - 1\) is given by \[X[k] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}nk}, 0 \le k \le N - 1\] Denote this relation as \(X = \text{DFT}(x)\). For \(N= 4\) which one of the following sequences satisfies DFT (DFT(x) ) = x ?
questions.explanation:
Given the modified N-point DFT equation with a unitary scaling factor: \[X[k] = rac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j rac{2\pi}{N}nk}\] Let \(y[n]\) be the output of applying the DFT twice, i.e., \(y = ext{DFT}( ext{DFT}(x))\). Using the definition, the second DFT operation is: \[y[m] = rac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k] e^{-j rac{2\pi}{N}km}\] Substituting the expression for \(X[k]\) into the equation for \(y[m]\): \[y[m] = rac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( rac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j rac{2\pi}{N}nk} ight) e^{-j rac{2\pi}{N}km}\] \[y[m] = rac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} e^{-j rac{2\pi}{N}k(n+m)}\] From the orthogonality property of complex exponentials, the inner summation evaluates to: \[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} e^{-j rac{2\pi}{N}k(n+m)} = egin{cases} N, & ext{if } (n+m) mod N = 0 \ 0, & ext{otherwise} \end{cases}\] The condition \((n+m) mod N = 0\) implies \(n = (-m) mod N\). Substituting this back yields: \[y[m] = rac{1}{N} \left( x[(-m) mod N] \cdot N ight) = x[(-m) mod N]\] The problem states that \( ext{DFT}( ext{DFT}(x)) = x\), which means \(y[m] = x[m]\). Thus, the sequence must satisfy: \[x[m] = x[(-m) mod N]\] This condition requires the sequence to be an even sequence. For \(N = 4\), expanding this gives: \[x[0] = x[0]\] \[x[1] = x[(-1) mod 4] = x[3]\] \[x[2] = x[(-2) mod 4] = x[2]\] \[x[3] = x[(-3) mod 4] = x[1]\] Therefore, any sequence satisfying the given condition must have its \(n=1\) and \(n=3\) elements equal, meaning \(x[1] = x[3]\). Checking the given options where \(\mathbf{x} = [x[0]\ x[1]\ x[2]\ x[3]]\): Option A: \(x[1] = 2, x[3] = 4 \implies x[1] eq x[3]\) Option B: \(x[1] = 2, x[3] = 2 \implies x[1] = x[3]\) (Satisfies the condition) Option C: \(x[1] = 3, x[3] = 2 \implies x[1] eq x[3]\) Option D: \(x[1] = 2, x[3] = 3 \implies x[1] eq x[3]\) Only the sequence in Option B satisfies the required symmetry. \[ oxed{ ext{B) $\mathbf{x} = [1\ 2\ 3\ 2]$ }}\]
Key points
  • The standard unscaled DFT of the DFT of a sequence yields \(N x[(-n) mod N]\).
  • For the unitary DFT defined with a \(1/\sqrt{N}\) scaling factor, applying the DFT twice yields exactly \(x[(-n) mod N]\).
  • The condition \(x[n] = x[(-n) mod N]\) defines a discrete-time even (or circularly symmetric) sequence.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A Fourier transform pair is given by \[\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n u[n + 3] \stackrel{FT}{\longleftrightarrow}\frac{A e^{j6\pi f}}{1 - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)e^{-j2\pi f}}\] where \(u(n)\) denotes the unit step sequence. The values of A is .
questions.explanation:
Given the discrete-time sequence: \[x[n] = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n u[n + 3]\] We can express this sequence in a form that allows us to use standard Fourier Transform pairs. We manipulate the expression to match the argument of the unit step function: \[x[n] = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-3} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n+3} u[n + 3]\] \[x[n] = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^3 \left[ \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n+3} u[n + 3] \right]\] \[x[n] = \frac{27}{8} \left[ \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{n+3} u[n + 3] \right]\] Let \(g[n] = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n u[n]\). The standard Fourier Transform of \(g[n]\) is: \[G(f) = \frac{1}{1 - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)e^{-j2\pi f}}\] Our signal \(x[n]\) can be written in terms of \(g[n]\) as: \[x[n] = \frac{27}{8} g[n + 3]\] Using the time-shifting property of the Fourier Transform, \(g[n - n_0] \stackrel{FT}{\longleftrightarrow} G(f) e^{-j2\pi f n_0}\). For a time advance of \(3\) (\(n_0 = -3\)), we get: \[g[n + 3] \stackrel{FT}{\longleftrightarrow} G(f) e^{j2\pi f (3)} = G(f) e^{j6\pi f}\] Therefore, the Fourier Transform of \(x[n]\) is: \[X(f) = \frac{27}{8} G(f) e^{j6\pi f} = \frac{3.375 e^{j6\pi f}}{1 - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)e^{-j2\pi f}}\] Comparing this result with the structure of the given Fourier Transform pair: \[X(f) = \frac{A e^{j6\pi f}}{1 - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)e^{-j2\pi f}}\] We find the value of \(A\): \[A = \frac{27}{8} = 3.375\] \[\boxed{3.375}\]
Key points
  • Standard Fourier Transform pair: \(a^n u[n] \stackrel{FT}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{1}{1 - a e^{-j2\pi f}}\) for \(|a| < 1\).
  • Time-shifting property: \(x[n-n_0] \stackrel{FT}{\longleftrightarrow} X(f) e^{-j2\pi f n_0}\). A time advance (where \(n_0\) is negative) results in a positive complex exponential phase shift.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: An N -type semiconductor having uniform doping is biased as shown in the figure. [figure unavailable] If \(E_C\) is the lowest energy level of the conduction band, \(E_V\) is the highest energy level of the valence band and \(E_F\) is the Fermi level, which one of the following represents the energy band diagram for the biased N-type semiconductor ?
questions.explanation: The bands tilt upward because electron energy is inversely related to electrostatic potential (\(E = -qV\)). Since the left side is connected to the negative terminal (lower potential), it has higher energy. This makes Option D the only diagram where \(E_{C}\), \(E_{F}\), and \(E_{V}\) correctly reflect this upward shift. \[\boxed{D}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Consider a silicon sample doped with \(N_D = 1 \times 10^{15} \text{ /cm}^3\) donor atoms. Assume that the intrinsic carrier concentration \(n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{10} \text{ /cm}^3\). If the sample is additionally doped with \(N_A = 1 \times 10^{18} \text{ /cm}^3\) acceptor atoms, the approximate number of electrons\(\text{/cm}^3\) in the sample, at T = \(300\) K, will be ______.
questions.explanation:
For a compensated \(p\)-type semiconductor, the minority carrier electron concentration is given by \[n_{o} = \frac{n_{i}^{2}}{(N_{A} - N_{D})}\] Substituting the given values: \[n_{o} = \frac{2.25 \times 10^{20}}{(10^{18} - 10^{15})} = 225\,\text{cm}^{-3}\] \[\boxed{225}\]
Key points
  • In a compensated semiconductor, the net carrier concentration is determined by the difference between acceptor and donor concentrations.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The cut-off wavelength (in \(\mu\) m) of light that can be used for intrinsic excitation of a semiconductor material of bandgap \(E_g = 1.1 \text{ eV}\) is ____.
questions.explanation:
The critical wavelength (\(\lambda_{c}\)) for a semiconductor, which corresponds to the minimum photon energy required to excite an electron across the bandgap, is calculated as follows: \[\lambda_{c} = \frac{1.242}{E_{g}(\text{eV})}\,\mu\text{m} = \frac{1.242}{1.1}\,\mu\text{m} = 1.129\,\mu\text{m}\] \[\boxed{1.129}\]
Key points
  • The relationship between photon wavelength and energy is derived from \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\).
  • When energy (\(E_{g}\)) is expressed in electron-volts (\(\text{eV}\)) and wavelength in micrometers (\(\mu\text{m}\)), the constant \(hc\) is approximately \(1.242\).
  • Photons with wavelengths longer than \(\lambda_{c}\) do not have sufficient energy to cause intrinsic excitation.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse \(\mu\text{m}\) with \(\text{nm}\); if using nanometers, the constant becomes \(1242\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: In the figure, \(ln(\rho_i)\) is plotted as a function of \(1/T\), where \(\rho_i\) is the intrinsic resistivity of silicon, \(T\) is the temperature, and the plot is almost linear. The slope of the line can be used to estimate [figure unavailable]
options: sum of electron and hole mobility in silicon (\(\mu_n + \mu_p\))
reciprocal of the sum of electron and hole mobility in silicon \((\mu_n + \mu_p)^{-1}\)
questions.explanation: Intrinsic resistivity \(\rho_i\) is inversely proportional to intrinsic carrier concentration \(n_i\), which varies as \(\exp(-E_g / 2kT)\). Plotting \(\ln(\rho_i)\) against \(1/T\) yields a line with a slope proportional to \(E_g / 2k\), allowing for the estimation of the bandgap energy. Thus Option A is correct. \[\boxed{(A) \text{ band gap energy of silicon (} E_g \text{)}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: At T = \(300\) K, the band gap and the intrinsic carrier concentration of GaAs are \(1.42\) eV and \(10^6 \text{ } cm^{-3}\), respectively. In order to generate electron hole pairs in GaAs, which one of the wavelength (\(\lambda_C\)) ranges of incident radiation, is most suitable ? (Given that : Plank's constant is \(6.62 \times 10^{-34}\)J-s, velocity of light is \(3 \times 10^{10} \text{ } cm/s\) and charge of electron is \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\)C)
questions.explanation:
The condition for a photon to be absorbed by a semiconductor and create an electron-hole pair is that its energy must be greater than or equal to the bandgap energy (\(E_{g}\)). This corresponds to a critical wavelength (\(\lambda_{c}\)) condition: \[\lambda_{c} \leq \frac{1.242}{E_{g}(\text{eV})}\,\mu\text{m}\] Given the bandgap energy \(E_{g} = 1.42\,\text{eV}\), we calculate the maximum allowable wavelength: \[\lambda_{c} \leq \frac{1.242}{1.42}\] \[\lambda_{c} \leq 0.87\,\mu\text{m}\] \[\boxed{(A) \, 0.42 \mu m < \lambda _c < 0.87 \mu m}\]
Key points
  • Absorption occurs only when the incident photon wavelength is shorter than or equal to the threshold wavelength.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: At T = \(300\) K, the hole mobility of a semiconductor \(\mu_P = 500 \text{ } cm^2 / Vs\) and \(\dfrac{KT}{q} = 26 \text{ } mV\). The hole diffusion constant \(D_P\) in \(cm^2 / s\) is ____.
questions.explanation: Using the Einstein relation for a semiconductor, the diffusion coefficient (\(D_{p}\)) and mobility (\(\mu_{p}\)) of holes are related to the thermal voltage (\(V_{T}\)) as follows: \[\frac{D_{p}}{\mu_{p}} = V_{T}\] Given the hole mobility \(\mu_{p} = 500\,\text{cm}^{2}/\text{V}\text{s}\) and assuming a thermal voltage \(V_{T} = 26\,\text{mV}\) at room temperature: \[D_{p} = \mu_{p}V_{T} = 500 \times 26 \times 10^{-3} = 13\,\text{cm}^{2}/\text{s}\] \[\boxed{13}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A thin P-type silicon sample is uniformly illuminated with light which generates excess carriers. The recombination rate is directly proportional to
questions.explanation: The recombination rate in a semiconductor is defined as \(R = \Delta n / \tau\), where \(\Delta n\) is the excess minority carrier concentration and \(\tau\) is the lifetime. This formula shows that the rate is directly proportional to D the excess minority carrier concentration. \[\boxed{(D) \text{ the excess minority carrier concentration}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Assume electronic charge \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ } C\), \(kT/q=25mV\) and electron mobility \(\mu_n = 1000 \text{ } cm^2 / V s\) . If the concentration gradient of electrons injected into a P-type silicon sample is \(1 \times 10^{21} \text{ } /cm^4\), the magnitude of electron diffusion current density (in \(A / cm^2\)) is ____.
questions.explanation: The electron diffusion current density is given by the relation: \[J = qD_{n} \frac{dn}{dx}\] where the electron diffusion coefficient \(D_{n}\) is determined using the Einstein relation: \[D_{n} = \mu_{n}V_{T}\] Given the values: \[D_{n} = \frac{1000\,\text{cm}^{2}}{\text{V}\text{ s}} \times 25 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{V} = 25\,\text{cm}^{2}/\text{s}\] Substituting the parameters into the current density formula: \[J = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 25 \times 1 \times 10^{21} = 4000\,\text{A}/\text{cm}^{2}\] \[\boxed{4000}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A silicon bar is doped with donor impurities \(N_D = 2.25 \times 10^{15} \text{ } atom/cm^3\). Given the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon at T = \(300\) K is \(n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{10} \text{ } cm^{-3}\). Assuming complete impurity ionization, the equilibrium electron and hole concentrations are
questions.explanation: Since \(N_{D} \gg n_{i}\), the equilibrium electron concentration is approximately equal to the donor concentration: \[n \simeq N_{D} = 2.25 \times 10^{5}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\] The equilibrium hole concentration is determined using the mass action law: \[p = \frac{n_{i}^{2}}{N_{D}} = \frac{(1.5 \times 10^{10})^{2}}{2.25 \times 10^{15}}  = 1 \times 10^{5}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\] \[\boxed{(D) \, n_0 = 2.25 \times 10^{15} \, cm^{-3} \, , p_0 = 1 \times 10^5 \, cm^{-3}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The donor and accepter impurities in an abrupt junction silicon diode are \(1 \times 10^{16}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) and \(5 \times 10^{18}\text{ cm}^{-3}\), respectively. Assume that the intrinsic carrier concentration in silicon \(n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{10}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) at \(300\text{ K}\), \(\dfrac{kT}{q} = 26\text{ mV}\) and the permittivity of silicon \(\varepsilon_{si} = 1.04 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}/\text{cm}\). The built-in potential and the depletion width of the diode under thermal equilibrium conditions, respectively, are
questions.explanation:
The built-in potential (\(V_{bi}\)) of a p-n junction is determined by the doping concentrations of the p and n sides and the intrinsic carrier concentration of the material. \[V_{bi} = V_{T} \ln \left[ \frac{N_{a} N_{d}}{n_{i}^{2}} \right]\] Substituting the given values: \[V_{bi} = 0.026 \ln \left[ \frac{10^{16} \times 5 \times 10^{18}}{2.25 \times 10^{20}} \right] = 0.86\,\text{V}\] The depletion width (\(W\)) at equilibrium is given by: \[W = \sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q} \left[ \frac{1}{N_{a}} + \frac{1}{N_{d}} \right] V_{bi}}\] \[W = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.04 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \left[ \frac{1}{5 \times 10^{18}} + \frac{1}{10^{16}} \right] \times 0.86}\] \[W = 3.3 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{cm}\] \[\boxed{(D)\, 0.86\,V \text{ and } 3.3\times 10^{-5} cm}\]
Key points
  • In a one-sided junction (\(N_{d} \gg N_{a}\)), the formula simplifies to \(W \approx \sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon V_{bi}}{q N_{a}}}\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Consider an abrupt PN junction (at \(T = 300\,\text{K}\)) shown in the figure. The depletion region width \(X_n\) on the N-side of the junction is \(0.2\,\mu\text{m}\) and the permittivity of silicon (\(\varepsilon_{si}\)) is \(1.044 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F}/\text{cm}\). At the junction, the approximate value of the peak electric field (in \(\text{kV}/\text{cm}\)) is ____. [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
For an abrupt \(P^{+}N\) junction, the doping concentration on the p-side (\(N_{a}\)) is much higher than the doping concentration on the n-side (\(N_{d}\)). Consequently, the depletion region extends almost entirely into the n-side. \[N_{a} \gg N_{d} \implies W \simeq x_{n}\] The maximum electric field (\(E_{max}\)) occurs at the junction (\(x = 0\)) and is given by: \[E_{max} = \frac{-q N_{d} x_{n}}{\epsilon_{s}}\] Substituting the given values into the equation: \[E_{max} = \frac{-1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{16} \times 0.2 \times 10^{-4}}{1.044 \times 10^{-12}} = -30.65 \times 10^{3}\,\text{V/cm}\] The peak value of the electric field is approximately \(-30.65\,\text{kV/cm}\). \[\boxed{-30.65}\]
Key points
  • The electric field is maximum at the metallurgical junction and decreases linearly to zero at the edges of the depletion region.
  • The negative sign indicates that the electric field vector points from the n-side (positive space charge) to the p-side (negative space charge).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: When a silicon diode having a doping concentration of \(N_A = 9 \times 10^{16} \text{ } cm^{-3}\) on p -side and \(N_D = 1 \times 10^{16} \text{ } cm^{-3}\) on n-side is reverse biased, the total depletion width is found to be \(3 \text{ } \mu \text{m}\). Given that the permittivity of silicon is \(1.04 \times 10^{-12}\) F/cm, the depletion width on the p-side and the maximum electric field in the depletion region, respectively, are
questions.explanation:
We know that the charge neutrality condition in a \(p\)-\(n\) junction relates the doping concentrations to the depletion widths: \[\frac{N_{A}}{N_{D}} = \frac{x_{n}}{x_{p}}\] Adding 1 to both sides to relate the total depletion width (\(W = x_{n} + x_{p}\)): \[\frac{N_{A}}{N_{D}} + 1 = \frac{x_{n}}{x_{p}} + 1 \implies \frac{N_{A} + N_{D}}{N_{D}} = \frac{x_{n} + x_{p}}{x_{p}}\] Substituting the given values (\(N_{A} + N_{D} \approx 10^{17}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\), \(N_{D} = 10^{16}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\), and \(W = 3\,\mu\text{m}\)): \[\frac{10^{17}}{10^{16}} = \frac{3\,\mu\text{m}}{x_{p}} \implies x_{p} = 0.3\,\mu\text{m}\] The maximum electric field (\(E_{\text{max}}\)) at the junction is given by: \[E_{\text{max}} = \frac{q N_{A} x_{p}}{\epsilon_{s}} = \frac{q N_{D} x_{n}}{\epsilon_{s}}\] Substituting the numerical values: \[E_{\text{max}} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 9 \times 10^{16} \times 0.3 \times 10^{-4}}{1.04 \times 10^{-12}}\] \[E_{\text{max}} = 4.15 \times 10^{5}\,\text{V}/\text{cm}\] \[\boxed{(B) \, 0.3 \mu m \text{ and } 4.15 * 10^5 V/cm}\]
Key points
  • Charge neutrality requires \(N_{A} x_{p} = N_{D} x_{n}\).
  • The electric field is maximum at the metallurgical junction (\(x = 0\)).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The doping concentrations on the p-side and n-side of a silicon diode are \(1 \times 10^{16} \text{ } cm^{-3}\) and \(1 \times 10^{17} \text{ } cm^{-3}\), respectively. A forward bias of \(0.3\) V is applied to the diode. At T=\(300\)K, the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon \(n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{10} \text{ } cm^{-3}\) and \(\dfrac{KT}{q} = 26 \text{ } mV\). The electron concentration at the edge of the depletion region on the p-side is
questions.explanation:
The electron concentration at the edge of the depletion region on the \(p\)-side under forward bias \(V_{f}\) is given by: \[n_{p} = n_{p0} \exp \left[ \frac{qV_{f}}{kT} \right]\] where the equilibrium minority electron concentration \(n_{p0}\) is: \[n_{p0} = \frac{n_{i}^{2}}{N_{A}}\] Substituting the given values: \[n_{p0} = \frac{(1.5 \times 10^{10})^{2}}{10^{16}} = 2.25 \times 10^{4}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\] We then have the carrier concentration at the edge: \[n_{p} = 2.25 \times 10^{4} \exp \left[ \frac{0.3}{0.026} \right] = 2.306 \times 10^{9}\,\text{cm}^{-3}\] \[\boxed{(A) \, 2.3 \times 10^9 cm^ {-3}}\]
Key points
  • Minority carrier concentration increases exponentially with forward bias voltage.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Consider two BJTs biased at the same collector current with area \(A_1 = 0.2\,\mu\text{m} \times 0.2\,\mu\text{m}\) and \(A_2 = 300\,\mu\text{m} \times 300\,\mu\text{m}\). Assuming that all other device parameters are identical, \(\text{kT/q} = 26\text{ mV}\), the intrinsic carrier concentration is \(1 \times 10^{10}\text{ cm}^{-3}\), and \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\), the difference between the base-emitter voltages (in \(\text{mV}\)) of the two BJTs (i.e., \(V_{BE1} - V_{BE2}\)) is ____.
questions.explanation:
The collector current of a BJT is given by: \[I_C = I_S \exp\left[\frac{V_{BE}}{\eta V_T}\right]\] For the two transistors: \[I_{C_1} = I_{S_1} \exp\left[\frac{V_{BE_1}}{\eta V_T}\right] \quad \cdots (i)\] \[I_{C_2} = I_{S_2} \exp\left[\frac{V_{BE_2}}{\eta V_T}\right] \quad \cdots (ii)\] Applying the given condition \(I_{C_1} = I_{C_2}\), equating \((i)\) and \((ii)\): \[I_{S_1} \exp\left[\frac{V_{BE_1}}{\eta V_T}\right] = I_{S_2} \exp\left[\frac{V_{BE_2}}{\eta V_T}\right]\] Rearranging: \[V_{BE_1} - V_{BE_2} = \eta V_T \ln\left[\frac{I_{S_2}}{I_{S_1}}\right]\] The question does not explicitly mention that the device is a Silicon BJT. The Silicon assumption may be inferred from the given intrinsic carrier concentration: \[n_i = 1 \times 10^{10} cm^{-3}\] which corresponds approximately to silicon at room temperature. For a Silicon BJT, the ideality factor \(\eta = 2\). Substituting \(I_{S_2}/I_{S_1} = (300 \times 300)/(0.2 \times 0.2)\) and \(V_T = 26\,\text{mV}\): \[V_{BE_1} - V_{BE_2} = 2 \times 26 \times \ln\left[\frac{300 \times 300}{0.2 \times 0.2}\right] = 52 \times 7.717 = 380.28\,\text{mV}\] \[\boxed{380.28}\]
Key points
  • The saturation current \(I_S \propto A\) (junction area), so \(\dfrac{I_{S_2}}{I_{S_1}} = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A BJT is biased in forward active mode. Assume \(V_{BE} = 0.7\text{ V}\), \(\text{kT/q} = 25\text{mV}\) and reverse saturation current \(I_S = 10^{-13}\text{ mA}\). The transconductance of the BJT (in \(\text{mA/V}\)) is ____.
questions.explanation: The transconductance of a BJT is given by: \[g_m = \frac{I_C}{V_T}\] First, computing the collector current using \(I_S = 10^{-13}\,\text{A}\) and \(V_{BE} = 0.7\,\text{V}\), \(V_T = 25\,\text{mV}\): \[I_C = I_S\, e^{V_{BE}/V_T} = 10^{-13} \times e^{\,0.7/0.025}= 0.144\,\text{mA}\] Substituting into the transconductance expression: \[g_m = \frac{I_C}{V_T} = \frac{0.144\,\text{mA}}{25\,\text{mV}} = 5.76\,\text{mA/V}\] \[\boxed{5.76}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: An ideal MOS capacitor has boron doping-concentration of \(10^{15}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) in the substrate. When a gate voltage is applied, a depletion region of width \(0.5\,\mu\text{m}\) is formed with a surface (channel) potential of \(0.2\text{ V}\). Given \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-14}\text{ F/cm}\) and the relative permittivities of silicon and silicon dioxide are \(12\) and \(4\), respectively, the peak electric field (in \(\text{V/}\mu\text{m}\)) in the oxide region is ____.
questions.explanation:
The peak electric field in the oxide region is related to the semiconductor electric field by: \[E_{ox} = \frac{\varepsilon_S}{\varepsilon_{ox}} E_S\] First, computing the semiconductor electric field \(E_S\): \[E_S = \frac{0.2 \times 2}{0.5} = 0.8\,\text{V/}\mu\text{m}\] Substituting \(\varepsilon_S/\varepsilon_{ox} = 12/4 = 3\) and \(E_S = 0.8\,\text{V/}\mu\text{m}\): \[E_{ox} = \frac{12}{4} \times 0.8 = 2.4\] \[\boxed{2.4}\]
Key points
  • The boundary condition at the oxide--semiconductor interface requires continuity of the normal component of electric displacement: \(\varepsilon_{ox} E_{ox} = \varepsilon_S E_S\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The slope of the \(I_D\) vs. \(V_{GS}\) curve of an n-channel MOSFET in linear regime is \(10^{-3}\,\Omega^{-1}\) at \(V_{DS} = 0.1\text{V}\). For the same device, neglecting channel length modulation, the slope of the \(\sqrt{I_D}\) vs. \(V_{GS}\) curve (in \(\sqrt{\text{A}}/\text{V}\)) under saturation regime is approximately ____.
questions.explanation:
In the linear (triode) region, the drain current is: \[I_D = K_n\left[(V_{GS} - V_{th})V_{DS} - \frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]\] Differentiating with respect to \(V_{GS}\): \[\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{GS}} = K_n V_{DS}\] Using the given values \(\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS} = 10^{-3}\) and \(V_{DS} = 0.1\,\text{V}\): \[\frac{10^{-3}}{0.1} = K_n \implies K_n = 10^{-2}\,\text{A/V}^2\] In the saturation region, the drain current is: \[I_D = \frac{K_n}{2}(V_{GS} - V_{th})^2\] Taking the square root: \[\sqrt{I_D} = \sqrt{\frac{K_n}{2}}\,(V_{GS} - V_{th})\] Differentiating with respect to \(V_{GS}\): \[\frac{\partial\sqrt{I_D}}{\partial V_{GS}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_n}{2}}\] Substituting \(K_n = 10^{-2}\): \[\frac{\partial\sqrt{I_D}}{\partial V_{GS}} = \sqrt{\frac{10^{-2}}{2}} = \sqrt{5 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.0707 \sqrt{\text{ A}} \text{/V}\] \[\boxed{ 0.0707}\]
Key points
  • \(K_n = \mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)\) is extracted from the linear region by exploiting \(\partial I_D/\partial V_{GS} = K_n V_{DS}\), which eliminates \(V_{th}\) from the calculation.
  • In saturation, \(\sqrt{I_D}\) is linear in \((V_{GS}-V_{th})\); the slope \(\partial\sqrt{I_D}/\partial V_{GS} = \sqrt{K_n/2}\) is a constant independent of bias point --- useful for graphical extraction of \(K_n\) and \(V_{th}\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A depletion type N-channel MOSFET is biased in its linear region for use as a voltage controlled resistor. Assume threshold voltage \(V_{TH} = -0.5\text{ V}\), \(V_{GS} = 2.0\text{ V}\), \(V_{DS} = 5\text{ V}\), \(W/L = 100\), \(C_{OX} = 10^{-8}\text{ F/cm}^2\) and \(\mu_n = 800\text{ cm}^2/\text{V}-\text{s}\). The value of the resistance of the voltage controlled resistor (in \(\Omega\) ) is ____.
questions.explanation:
The voltage-controlled resistance \(r_{DS}\) in the linear region is given by: \[r_{DS} = \frac{1}{\mu_n C_{ox} \left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)(V_{GS} - V_t)}\] Substituting \(\mu_n C_{ox} = 800 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{A/V}^2\), \(W/L = 100\), and \(V_{GS} - V_t = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5\,\text{V}\): \[r_{DS} = \frac{1}{800 \times 10^{-8} \times 100 \times (2 + 0.5)} = \frac{1}{2 \times 10^{-3}} = 500 \Omega\] \[\boxed{500}\]
Key points
  • In the deep linear (triode) region where \(V_{DS} \ll V_{GS} - V_t\), the MOSFET behaves as a voltage-controlled resistor: \(r_{DS} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS}-V_t)}\).
  • \(r_{DS}\) is inversely proportional to \((V_{GS} - V_t)\); increasing \(V_{GS}\) reduces \(r_{DS}\), making the channel more conductive.
  • A larger \(W/L\) ratio directly reduces \(r_{DS}\), which is why wide short-channel devices are used as low-resistance switches.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: If fixed positive charges are present in the gate oxide of an n-channel enhancement type MOSFET, it will lead to
options: a decrease in the threshold voltage
an increase in substrate leakage current
questions.explanation:
The threshold voltage of an n-channel enhancement MOSFET is given by: \[V_T = \phi_{ms} - \frac{Q_{ox}}{C_{ox}} - \frac{Q'_d}{C_{ox}} + 2\phi_F\] Fixed positive charges \(Q_{ox} > 0\) present in the gate oxide contribute a negative term \(-Q_{ox}/C_{ox}\) to \(V_T\). Therefore, the presence of fixed positive oxide charges decreases the threshold voltage. For an n-channel enhancement MOSFET, a lower \(V_T\) means the device turns on at a smaller gate voltage --- in extreme cases, fixed oxide charges can even convert an enhancement-mode device into a depletion-mode device. Options B, C, and D are incorrect:
  • Channel-length modulation is caused by \(V_{DS}\) variation, not oxide charge.
  • Substrate leakage current is unrelated to fixed oxide charges.
  • Accumulation capacitance \(C_{ox} = \varepsilon_{ox}/t_{ox}\) depends only on oxide thickness and permittivity, not on fixed charge.
\[\boxed{(A)\text{ A decrease in the threshold voltage}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: When the optical power incident on a photodiode is \(10\,\mu\text{W}\) and the responsivity is \(0.8\text{ A/W}\), the photocurrent generated (in \(\mu\text{A}\)) is ____.
questions.explanation: Responsivity \(R\) is related to photocurrent \(I_{ph}\) and incident power \(P_{in}\) as \[R = \frac{I_{ph}}{P_{in}}\] Thus photocurrent can be obtained as: \[I_{ph} = R \times P_{in} = 0.8 A/W \times 10 \mu W = 8 \mu A\] \[\boxed{8}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the figure, assume that the forward voltage drops of the PN diode \(D_1\) and Schottky diode \(D_2\) are \(0.7 \text{ V}\) and \(0.3 \text{ V}\), respectively. If ON denotes conducting state of the diode and OFF denotes non-conducting state of the diode, then in the circuit,
questions.explanation:
Given : (i) Voltage drop of PN diode = \(0.7\,\text{V}\). (ii) Voltage drop of Schottky diode = \(0.3\,\text{V}\).
Method 1
(i) Assume both diodes \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) are ON. (ii) For both diodes to be ON, \(I_{D_1}\) and \(I_{D_2}\) should be greater than zero (\(I_{D} > 0\) from \(p\) to \(n\)). Applying KVL in the loop (1), \[-10 + 1 \times I + 0.7 = 0\] \[I = 9.3\,\text{mA}\] Applying KVL in the loop (2), \[-0.7 + 0.02 \times I_{D_2} + 0.3 = 0\] \[I_{D_2} = \frac{0.4}{0.02} = 20\,\text{mA}\] \[I_{D_1} = I - I_{D_2} = 9.3 - 20 = -10.7\,\text{mA}\] Since, \(I_{D_1} < 0\) and \(I_{D_2} > 0\) therefore, this assumption is not correct and \(D_{1}\) is OFF and \(D_{2}\) is ON. \[\boxed{\text{(D)}\quad D_1 \text{ is OFF and }D_2\text{ is ON}}\]
Method 2
(i) Assume both diodes \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) are OFF. (ii) For both diodes to be OFF, \(V_{D_1}\) should be less than \(0.7\,\text{V}\) and \(V_{D_2}\) should be less than \(0.3\,\text{V}\) (from \(p\) to \(n\)). From figure, \[V_{D_2} = 10\,\text{V}\] So \(D_2\) is ON and the moment \(D_2\) becomes ON, it is replaced by 0.3V source and the circuit becomes, Applying KVL in the above loop, \[-10 + I + 0.02I + 0.3 = 0\] \[I = \frac{10 - 0.3}{1.02\text{k}} = 9.50\,\text{mA}\] \[I_{D_2} = I = 9.50\,\text{mA}\] \[\therefore V_{D_1} = I \times 0.02 + 0.3\] \[V_{D_1} = 9.50\text{m} \times 0.02\text{k} + 0.3 = 0.49\,\text{V}\] Hence, \(V_{D_1} < 0.7\,\text{V}\) Therefore, this assumption is correct and diode \(D_{1}\) is OFF. \[\boxed{\text{(D)}\quad D_1 \text{ is OFF and }D_2\text{ is ON}}\]
Key points
  • For a diode assumed to be ON, replace it with its respective forward voltage drop (\(V_{on}\)) and verify that the calculated current flows from the p-type to n-type material (\(I_{D} > 0\)).
  • For a diode assumed to be OFF, replace it with an open circuit and verify that the voltage across its terminals (\(V_{p} - V_{n}\)) is less than its cut-in voltage (\(V_{D} < V_{on}\)).
  • If an assumed state leads to a contradiction in verification, the assumption is incorrect, and the alternative state must be analyzed.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Check the resistance units carefully.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The diode in the circuit shown has \(V_{on} = 0.7\text{ Volts}\) but is ideal otherwise. If \(V_i = 5 \sin(\omega t)\text{Volts}\), the minimum and maximum values of \(V_o\) (in Volts) are, respectively,
questions.explanation:
Given :
(i) \(V_{on} = 0.7\,\text{V} , V_{i} = 5\sin(\omega t)\,\text{V}\)
(ii) \(V_{i(\text{max})} = \left. 5\sin\omega t \right|_{\text{max}} = +5\,\text{V}\)
(iii) \(V_{i(\text{min})} = \left. 5\sin\omega t \right|_{\text{min}} = -5\,\text{V}\) Case 1 : \(\mathbf{V_{i(\text{max})} = +5\,\text{V}}\) , Diode will be forward biased, hence it can be replaced by its cut-in voltage i.e. \(V_{on}\). Applying KVL in above figure, \[I = \frac{5 - 0.7 - 2}{2} = \frac{2.3}{2}\] \[V_{o} = \frac{2.3}{2} \times 1 + 0.7 + 2 = 3.85\,\text{V}\] Case 2 : \(\mathbf{V_{i} = -5\,\text{V}}\) , Diode will be reverse biased, hence it can be replaced by open circuit. From the above circuit, \(V_{o} = V_{i} = -5\,\text{V}\) From Case 1 and Case 2, \[V_{o} = \begin{cases} V_{o(\text{max})} = 3.85\,\text{V} & ; \quad V_{i} = +5\,\text{V} \\ V_{o(\text{min})} = -5\,\text{V} & ; \quad V_{i} = -5\,\text{V} \end{cases}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\quad \text{-5 and 3.85}}\]
Key points
  • To find the maximum and minimum output voltages in a clipping circuit, evaluate the circuit at the positive and negative peaks of the input signal.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The figure shows a half-wave rectifier. The diode \(D\) is ideal. The average steady-state current (in Amperes) through the diode is approximately __________.
questions.explanation:
Case 1: During Positive half cycle of input, when the input voltage is rising to its peak, the diode becomes ON and the capacitor starts charging. When diode is ON, the charging time constant is given by, Charging time constant, \(\tau_{C} = R_{TH}C = 0\,\text{sec}\)
Since time constant is zero, the capacitor will take no time to charge and it will follow the input waveform till point A. Case 2: When the input starts falling from its peak value, the diode will be off as the input goes below 10 V and capacitor is holding 10 V. When diode is OFF, discharging time constant is given by, \[\tau_{D} = R_{TH}C = RC\] \[\tau_{D} = 100 \times 4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{sec}\] \[\tau_{D} = 400\,\text{msec}\] Time period of input signal is given by, \[T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{50} = 20\,\text{msec} \,\text{[Given, } f = 50\,\text{Hz]}\] Since, \(T \ll \tau_{D}\), the capacitor starts discharging slowly through the resistor till point B as shown in the figure until the next positive input cycle arrives. Now the capacitor starts charging again upto the peak value of input (point A) and this process continues.
Method 1
The current through the diode is given by \[I_{D}(t) = I_{R}(t) + I_{C}(t)\] \[I_{D}(t) = \frac{V_{C}(t)}{R} + C \frac{dV_{C}(t)}{dt}\] The average value of current is \[\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} I_{D}(t) dt = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} \frac{V_{C}(t)}{R} dt + \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} C \frac{dV_{C}(t)}{dt} dt\] At steady state, \(V_{C}(t)\) is a periodic waveform with period \(T\), it can be expressed in Fourier series as \[V_{C}(t) = V_{0} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( A_{n} \cos(n\omega t) + B_{n} \sin(n\omega t) \right)\] where \(V_{0}\) is the DC or average value. \[\frac{dV_{C}(t)}{dt} = 0 + \frac{d}{dt} \left( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( A_{n} \cos(n\omega t) + B_{n} \sin(n\omega t) \right) \right)\] Hence we can say that the derivative of any periodic waveform has zero DC value or Average value. \[\therefore \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} \frac{dV_{C}(t)}{dt} dt = 0\] or we can say that at steady state, the average value of current through capacitor is zero. Now, the average value of diode current is \[(I_{D})_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} \frac{V_{C}(t)}{R} dt + 0\] As the capacitor is discharging very slowly, we can approximately say that, capacitor is holding a value \(10\,\text{V}\), throughout its time period. \[\therefore (I_{D})_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} \frac{10}{R} dt = \frac{10}{R \cdot T} \int_{0}^{T} dt = \frac{10T}{RT} = \frac{10}{R} = 0.1\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{\text{The average steady state current is 0.1A}}\]
Method 2
The voltage across capacitor at steady state looks approximately like a DC with a small triangular ripple superimposed. Maximum output voltage = \(V_m\) = 10 V Minimum output voltage = \(V_m - V_{r(p-p)}\) Then the average value is approximately the middle point of these two values. \[V_{dc} = \frac{{}V_{m} + (V_m- V_{r\,(p-p)})}{2}\] \[V_{dc} = V_{m} - \frac{V_{r\,(p-p)}}{2}\] Where, \(V_{r\,(p-p)}\) is the peak to peak ripple voltage and it is the amount by which capacitor voltage falls before charging again. \[V_{r\,(p-p)} = \frac{I_{dc}}{fC}\] \[\therefore I_{dc}R_{L} = V_{m} - \frac{I_{dc}}{2fC}\] \[I_{dc} \left[ R_{L} + \frac{1}{2fC} \right] = V_{m}\] \[I_{dc} = \frac{V_{m}}{R_{L} + \frac{1}{2fC}} = \frac{10}{100 + \frac{1}{2 \times 50 \times 4 \times 10^{-3}}}\] \[I_{dc} = 0.09 \approx 0.1\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{\text{The average steady state current is 0.1A}}\]
Key points
  • The average DC voltage across the load is approximated as \(V_{dc} = V_{m} - \frac{V_{r\,p-p}}{2}\), where \(V_{r\,p-p} \approx \frac{I_{dc}}{fC}\) is the peak-to-peak ripple voltage for a half-wave rectifier.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: Two silicon diodes, with a forward voltage drop of \(0.7\,\text{V}\), are used in the circuit shown in the figure. The range of input voltage \(V_i\) for which the output voltage \(V_o = V_i\), is
questions.explanation: In the given circuit make the diodes ideal and add their cutin voltages to the voltage sources directly and the circuit becomes Case 1 : During positive half cycle, Diode \(D_{1}\) will be reverse biased and hence, \(D_{1}\) will act as open circuit. (a) \(\mathbf{0 < V_{i} < 2.7\,\text{V}}\) : Diode \(D_{2}\) will be reversed biased and hence, it acts as open circuit. Applying KVL, \(-V_{i} + 0\,\text{V} + V_{0} = 0\) Hence, \(V_{0} = V_{i}\) (b) \(\mathbf{V_{i} > 2.7\,\text{V}}\) : Diode \(D_{2}\) will be forward biased and hence, it can be replaced by cut-in voltage \(V_{\gamma}\). Applying KVL, \(-2.7\,\text{V} + V_{0} = 0\) Hence, \(V_{0} = 2.7\,\text{V}\) Case 2 : During negative half cycle, Diode \(D_{2}\) will be reverse biased and hence, \(D_{2}\) will act as open circuit. (a) \(\mathbf{-1.7\,\text{V} < V_{i} < 0\,\text{V}}\) : Diode \(D_{1}\) will be reverse biased and hence it acts as open circuit. Applying KVL, \(-V_{i} + 0\,\text{V} + V_{0} = 0\implies V_{0} = V_{i}\) (b) \(\mathbf{V_{i} < -1.7\,\text{V}}\) : Diode \(D_{1}\) will be forward biased and hence it can be replaced by cut-in voltage \(V_{\gamma}\). Applying KVL in the above circuit, \(-1.7\,\text{V} + V_{0} = 0\) Hence, \(V_{0} = -1.7\,\text{V}\) Hence, from Case 1 and Case 2, expression of output voltage can be written as given below, \[V_{0} = \begin{cases} V_{i} & ; \quad 0\,\text{V} \leq V_{i} < 2.7\,\text{V} \\ 2.7\,\text{V} & ; \quad V_{i} \geq 2.7\,\text{V} \\ V_{i} & ; \quad -1.7\,\text{V} < V_{i} \leq 0\,\text{V} \\ -1.7\,\text{V} & ; \quad V_{i} \leq -1.7\,\text{V} \end{cases}\] Hence, the output waveform is shown below, Therefore when \(-1.7 < V_{i} < 2.7\), then both \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) are OFF and hence \(V_{0} = V_{i}\). \[\boxed{\text{(D) -1.7 V} < V_i <\text{ 2.7 V}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A good current buffer has
options: low input impedance and low output impedance
low input impedance and high output impedance
high input impedance and low output impedance
high input impedance and high output impedance
questions.explanation:
A current buffer is a specialized electronic amplifier that converts an input current signal into an output current signal. A good current buffer should have Low input impedance and high output impedance Reason: The generic diagram of a current buffer is shown below. Importance of Low Input Impedance: Efficient Current Transfer: To efficiently capture the input current most of the input current should flow into the amplifier(\(R_{i}\)) for which \(R_{i}\) should be as low as possible(so that using current division rule most of the current goes into \(R_{i}\)). Importance of High Output Impedance Driving loads effectively: In order to drive the load efficiently most of the output current should flow into load for which \(R_{0}\) should be as high as possible (so that using current division rule most of the current flows into load). \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\quad \text{low input impedance and high output impedance}}\]
Key points
  • Current Amplifier: Input = Current, Output = Current \(\rightarrow\) Low \(Z_{in}\), High \(Z_{out}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the ac equivalent circuit shown in the figure, if \(i_{in}\) is the input current and \(R_F\) is very large, the type of feedback is
questions.explanation:
Given circui is, Since the input signal is an input current \(i_{in}\), the feedback signal mixes in shunt at the input. Hence, the input mixing is current mixing. Also, the feedback resistor \(R_F\) is directly connected from the output node back to the input node, i.e. the sampled quantity is output voltage. Hence, the feedback topology is voltage shunt feedback or voltage current feedback. \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\quad \text{voltage-current feedback}}\]
Key points
  • Shunt connection at input \(\Rightarrow\) current mixing.
  • Feedback element directly connected to output node \(\Rightarrow\) Voltage sampling.
Mistakes to avoid
  • \(R_F\) connected across the output node implies voltage sensing, not current sensing.
  • Do not reverse the answer. Output topology comes first in the answer.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A depletion type N-channel MOSFET is biased in its linear region for use as a voltage controlled resistor. Assume threshold voltage \(V_{\text{TH}} = -0.5\,\text{V}\), \(V_{\text{GS}} = 2.0\,\text{V}\), \(V_{\text{DS}} = 5\,\text{V}\), \(W/L = 100\), \(C_{\text{ox}} = 10^{-8}\,\text{F/cm}^2\) and \(\mu_n = 800\,\text{cm}^2\text{/V-s}\). The value of the resistance of the voltage controlled resistor (in \(\Omega\)) is _________.
questions.explanation: For a MOSFET in the linear region: \(V_{GS} > V_{th}\) and \(V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{th}\) The current equation for a MOSFET in the saturation region is given by: \[I_D = \mu C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} \left\{ (V_{GS} - V_{th})V_{DS} - \frac {V_{DS}^2}{2} \right\}\] Taking the derivative of the above w.r.t. \(V_{DS}\), we get: \[\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{DS}} = \mu C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right) (V_{GS} - V_{TH} - V_{DS})\] Voltage-controlled Resistor (\(r_{DS}\)) is defined as: \[r_{DS} = \left | \frac{\partial V_{DS}}{\partial I_{DS}}\right| = \left |\frac{1}{\mu_n C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right) (V_{GS} - V_{TH} - V_{DS})} \right |\] Given: \(V_{GS} = 2.0\,\text{V}\), \(V_{TH} = -0.5\,\text{V}\), \(\frac{W}{L} = 100\), \(C_{ox} = 10^{-8}\,\text{F/cm}^2\), \(\mu_n = 800\,\text{cm}^2\text{/V-s}\), \(V_{DS} = 5\,\text{V}\) Putting on the respective values in above equation, we get: \[r_{DS} = \left | \frac{1}{800 \times 10^{-8} \times 100 \times (2 - (-0.5)-5)} \right|\] \[\boxed{r_{DS} = 500\,\Omega}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: For the n-channel MOS transistor shown in the figure, the threshold voltage \(V_{Th}\) is \(0.8\text{ V}\). Neglect channel length modulation effects. When the drain voltage \(V_D = 1.6\text{ V}\), the drain current \(I_D\) was found to be \(0.5\text{ mA}\). If \(V_D\) is adjusted to be \(2\text{ V}\) by changing the values of \(R\) and \(V_{DD}\), the new value of \(I_D\) (in mA) is
questions.explanation: Given \(V_{Th} = 0.8\,\text{V}\), \(V_{D_1} = 1.6\,\text{V}, \quad I_{D_1} = 0.5\,\text{mA}\), \(V_{D_2} = 2\,\text{V}, \quad I_{D_2} = ?\), Since the drain and gate of the MOSFET are shorted, it is in saturation. The saturation current equation neglecting channel length modulation is given by, \[I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_T)^2\] \[I_D = \frac{1}{2} K_N \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_T)^2\] For \(V_D = 1.6v\) \[I_{D_1} = k_n(V_{GS_1} - V_T)^2\] \[k_n = \frac{I_{D_1}}{(1.6 - 0.8)^2} = \frac{0.5}{(0.8)^2}\] \[k_n = 0.78\,\text{mA/v}\] For \(V_{D_2} =V_{GS_2} = 2\,\text{V}\), \[I_{D_2} = k_n(V_{GS_2} - V_T)^2\] \[I_{D_2} = 0.78 (2 - 0.8)^2\] \[I_{D_2} = 1.125\,\text{mA}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\quad 1.125}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: For the MOSFETs shown in the figure, the threshold voltage \(|V_t| = 2\text{ V}\) and \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}\mu C_{ox}\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right) = 0.1\text{ mA/V}^2\). The value of \(I_D\) (in mA) is _________.
questions.explanation: From the below figure, \(V_{G2} = 0\) Since the gate of MOSFET does not draw any current, we can apply voltage division rule at resistive divider to get \(V_{G1}\) \[V_{G1} = V_{DD} \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} \right)\] \[= 12 \times \frac{10}{10+10} = 6\,\text{V}\] Here both MOSFETs will be in saturation as, For \(M_2\) to be in saturation, \[V_{DS2} > V_{GS2} - V_t\] \[V_x > 0 - (-5)-2 \implies V_x > 3V\] For \(M_1\) to be in saturation \[V_{SD1} > V_{GS1} - |V_t|\] \[12-V_x > (12-6) -2\implies V_x < 8V\] Since there is a valid range of \(V_x\) both MOSFETs will be in saturation. Drain current \(= I_{D1} = I_{D2} = I_D\) \[I_{D} = \frac{1}{2} \mu C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_T)^2\] \[I_{D} = \frac{1}{2} \mu C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS2} - V_T)^2 = 0.1 \times [(0-(-5)) - 2]^2 = 0.9\] \[= 0.1 \times [5 - 2]^2 = 0.9\,\text{mA}\] \[\boxed{I_D=0.9\,\text{mA}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The desirable characteristics of a transconductance amplifier are
options: high input resistance and high output resistance
high input resistance and low output resistance
low input resistance and high output resistance
low input resistance and low output resistance
questions.explanation:
A transconductance amplifier is a specialized electronic amplifier that converts an input voltage signal into an output current signal. A good transconductance amplifier should have high input impedance and high output impedance Reason: The generic diagram of a transconductance amplifier is shown below. Importance of High Input Impedance: Efficient Voltage Transfer: To efficiently capture the input voltage most of the input voltage should be dropped acorss \(R_i\) for which \(R_{i}\) should be as high as possible(so that using voltage division rule most of the voltage drops across \(R_{i}\)). Importance of High Output Impedance Driving loads effectively: In order to drive the load efficiently most of the output current should flow into load for which \(R_{0}\) should be as high as possible (so that using current division rule most of the current flows into load). \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\quad \text{high input resistance and high output resistance}}\]
Key points
  • Transconductance Amplifier: Input = Voltage, Output = Current \(\rightarrow\) High \(Z_{in}\), High \(Z_{out}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The slope of the \(I_D\) vs. \(V_{GS}\) curve of an n-channel MOSFET in linear regime is \(10^{-3}\Omega^{-1}\) at \(V_{DS} = 0.1\text{ V}\). For the same device, neglecting channel length modulation, the slope of the \(\sqrt{I_D}\) vs. \(V_{GS}\) curve (in \(\sqrt{\text{A}}/\text{V}\)) under saturation regime is approximately __________.
questions.explanation:
Given \[\frac{\partial I_{DS}}{\partial V_{GS}} = 10^{-3}\] Also, the MOSFET is operating in the linear region with \(V_{DS} = 0.1\,\text{V}\) The current in linear region neglecting channel length modulation is given by, \[I_{DS} = \mu_n C_0 \times \frac{W}{L} \left[ (V_{GS} - V_t)V_{DS} - \frac{V_{DS}^2}{2} \right]\] \[I_{DS} = K_n \left[ (V_{GS} - V_t)V_{DS} - \frac{V_{DS}^2}{2} \right]\] \[\frac{\partial I_{DS}}{\partial V_{GS}} = K_n V_{DS}\] \[10^{-3} = K_n (0.1)\] \[K_n = 10^{-2}\] Now, the current in saturation region is given by, \[I_{DS} = \frac{K_n}{2} [V_{GS} - V_t]^2\] \[\sqrt{I_{DS}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_n}{2}} (V_{GS} - V_t)\] Slope is nothing but the rate of change or the derivative, so \[\frac{\partial \sqrt{I_{DS}}}{\partial V_{GS}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_n}{2}}\] Putting on the respective values, we get: \[\text{Slope } =\frac{\partial \sqrt{I_{DS}}}{\partial V_{GS}}= \sqrt{\frac{10^{-2}}{2}} = 0.0707\,\sqrt{\text{A}}/\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{Slope}=0.0707\,\sqrt{\text{A}}/\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • To find slope we have to find the derivative of current with respect to voltage.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: For the MOSFET \(M_1\) shown in the figure, assume \(W/L = 2\), \(V_{DD} = 2.0\text{ V}\), \(\mu_n C_{ox} = 100\,\mu\text{A/V}^2\) and \(V_{TH} = 0.5\text{ V}\). The transistor \(M_1\) switches from saturation region to linear region when \(V_{in}\) (in Volts) is __________.
questions.explanation:
Given \(\frac{W}{L} = 2\), \(\mu_n C_{ox} = 100\,\mu\text{A/V}^2\), \(V_{th} = 0.5\,\text{V}\) For transition from saturation to linear region, \[V_{DS}=V_{GS}-V_T\] Since, \(V_{GS}=V_{in}\), \(V_{DS}=V_{out}\), \[V_{out}=V_{in}-0.5\] Current through the resistor is \[I_D=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R}\] \[I_D=\frac{2-(V_{in}-0.5)}{10^4}\] \[I_D=\frac{2.5-V_{in}}{10^4}\] At the boundary condition, \[I_D=\frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2\] \[I_D=\frac{1}{2}(100\times10^{-6})(2)(V_{in}-0.5)^2\] \[I_D=100\times10^{-6}(V_{in}-0.5)^2\] Equating the two expressions of current, \[100\times10^{-6}(V_{in}-0.5)^2=\frac{2.5-V_{in}}{10^4}\] \[(V_{in}-0.5)^2=2.5-V_{in}\] \[V_{in}^2-V_{in}+0.25=2.5-V_{in}\] \[V_{in}^2+0.25=2.5\] \[V_{in}^2=2.25\] \[\boxed{V_{in}=1.5~V}\]
Key points
  • At the boundary of saturation and linear region, \(V_{DS} = V_{GS} - V_{th}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the low-pass filter shown in the figure, for a cut-off frequency of \(5\text{ kHz}\) , the value of \(R_2\) (in \(\text{k}\Omega\)) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given, \[Z_1 = R_1\] \[Z_2 = R_2 || C = \frac{R_2\left(\frac{1}{j\omega C}\right)}{R_2 + \frac{1}{j\omega C}} = \frac{R_2}{1 + j\omega R_2 C}\] For the inverting amplifier: \[\frac{V_o}{V_i} = -\frac{Z_2}{Z_1}\] \[\frac{V_o}{V_i} = \frac{-\frac{R_2}{1 + j\omega R_2 C}}{R_1} = -\frac{(R_2/R_1)}{1 + j\omega R_2 C}\] The magnitude of the voltage gain will be: \[\left| \frac{V_o}{V_i} \right| = \frac{(R_2/R_1)}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega R_2 C)^2}}\] At \(\omega = 0\):
\[A_{max}=\left| \frac{V_o}{V_i} \right| = \frac{R_2}{R_1}\] \[\therefore \frac{V_o}{V_i} = \frac{A_{max}}{1 + j\omega R_2 C}\] \[\left| \frac{V_o}{V_i} \right| = \frac{A_{max}}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega R_2 C)^2}}\] At \(\omega = \omega_c\) (Cut-off frequency)
\[\left| \frac{V_o}{V_i} \right| = \frac{A_{max}}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[\frac{A_{max}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{A_{max}}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega_c R_2 C)^2}}\] \[2 = 1 + (\omega_c R_2 C)^2\] \[1 = \omega_c R_2 C\] \[\omega_c = \frac{1}{R_2 C}\] \[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R_2 C}\] \[R_2 = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 5 \times 10^3 \times 10 \times 10^{-9}}\] \[\boxed{R_2 = 3.18\,\text{k}\Omega}\]
Key points
  • Cut-off Frequency (\(f_c\)): The frequency at which the gain magnitude drops to \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of its maximum (DC) value. It is determined exclusively by the feedback network components: \(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R_2 C}\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the circuit shown, the op-amp has finite input impedance, infinite voltage gain and zero input offset voltage. The output voltage \(V_{\text{out}}\) is
questions.explanation:
Given, (i) \(R_i\) is finite i.e. internal input current exists. (ii) \(A_{OL}\) is infinite i.e. virtual ground concept is valid. (iii) \(V_{ios} = 0\) i.e. output voltage due to offset voltage does not exist. Given circuit is shown below, From virtual ground concept, \(V_+ = V_- = 0\) Applying KCL at inverting terminal, \[\frac{0}{R_1} + \frac{0 - V_{out}}{R_2} + I_1 = 0\] \[{V_{out} = I_1R_2}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)\quad}I_1R_2}\]
Key points
  • Unlike a completely ideal op-amp, an op-amp with finite input impedance will have non-zero currents (\(I_1\), \(I_2\)) flowing into its input terminals.
